newsitem.title: CHINA: HK top court to rule on China-installed parliament.
newsitem.headline: HK top court to rule on China-installed parliament.

text.p: An appeal court will hold a hearing on whether the legislature China installed in Hong Kong last week is legal, a spokesman said on Tuesday.

The hearing, set for July 29, was prompted by lawyers' challenges to the Provisional Legislature and to existing laws during a court case last week. The lawyers sought to halt a criminal trial on grounds that a legal vacuum exists.
A spokesman for the Justice Department said the arguments would be put to the Court of Appeal at the end of this month.

Lawyers have argued that laws passed by the interim legislature shortly before the sovereignty handover were illegal or that the pre-handover legal system was no longer valid because the new legislature had not adopted it.
The new unelected legislature, appointed by China, was sworn in a week ago, hours after Britain handed its 156-year-old colony back to Beijing as a special Chinese region.
The legislature has been controversial since its birth last December. Before last week's flag change it had met across the border in China to avoid legal challenges to its existence.
During that period the assembly enacted a string of laws including a rollback of some of Hong Kong's basic freedoms.
On handover night, it enacted an omnibus law validating all the legislation it had prepared before the handover.
China and the new Hong Kong government envisage the interim chamber sitting until a new legislature is constituted by elections some time next year.
However, arguments have been thrown up by legal experts and lawyers' groups suggesting that the body is unconstitutional.
If the Provisional Legislature were found to be illegal, this could plunge Hong Kong into legal chaos and possibly a constitutional crisis, legal experts said.
The Justice Department said the decision to hold an appeal hearing on the issue did not mean ongoing court cases should be adjourned pending the ruling.
"The Department of Justice is concerned that judicial proceedings should continue without delay while the issue is being resolved," the spokesman said.
